subject: Biology
title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
summary: How a cell duplicates its genome and divides: the phases of the cell cycle (G<sub>1</sub>, S, G<sub>2</sub>, M and G<sub>0</sub>), the four stages of mitosis plus cytokinesis, the two divisions of meiosis with the five substages of prophase I, and why each type of division matters. It is the last chapter of the Cell unit, a fixed source of diagram and difference questions in the school final, and one of the highest-yield chapters for NEET.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. This chapter closes Unit III, Cell: Structure and Function, which carries 15 marks shared with Cell: The Unit of Life and Biomolecules. In a typical school final the chapter alone is worth about 5 to 7 marks: one or two 1-mark items (a stage name, G<sub>0</sub>, the enzyme recombinase), a 2-mark difference (karyokinesis versus cytokinesis, anaphase versus anaphase I), a 3-mark question on interphase or prophase I, and very often a 5-mark question asking you to draw and describe the stages of mitosis or meiosis I. In NEET it is one of the most dependable chapters, with one to three questions nearly every year lifted almost word for word from NCERT.

question_types.note: Match the event to the stage: synaptonemal complex (zygotene), recombination nodules and recombinase (pachytene), chiasmata and the long pause in oocytes (diplotene), terminalisation (diakinesis), kinetochore attachment (metaphase), centromere splitting (anaphase, anaphase II but not anaphase I). Also: the duration of the human cell cycle and of M phase, the stage best for studying chromosome morphology, what doubles in S phase (DNA, not chromosome number), and the cell type in which mitosis happens in haploids (male honey bee).

Meiosis is reductional because homologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids, separate in anaphase I; S phase doubles DNA but not chromosome number; interkinesis has no S phase; metaphase chromosomes are the most condensed; cell plate forms from the centre outward in plants; G<sub>0</sub> cells are metabolically active but do not divide.

Define G<sub>0</sub>, interkinesis, synapsis, bivalent, chiasma; distinguish karyokinesis from cytokinesis; give two differences between cytokinesis in plant and animal cells; state the average cell cycle span of a mammalian cell; name the stage for each of four listed events (NCERT exercise 6).

Describe the events of interphase; explain why mitosis is called equational division and meiosis reductional; describe the events of pachytene or diplotene; compare anaphase of mitosis with anaphase I; describe cytokinesis in plants; state the significance of mitosis or of meiosis with three points.

Draw and describe the four stages of mitosis with labelled diagrams; describe the five substages of prophase I with a diagram of synapsis, bivalent and chiasmata; describe meiosis II and explain how it resembles mitosis; tabulate the differences between mitosis and meiosis; track chromosome number and DNA content through the whole cycle for a given cell.

A passage or figure showing a cell with a stated chromosome number or DNA content at one phase, followed by questions asking the chromosome number and DNA content at other phases, which division or stage is shown in a sketch, and one reasoning question such as why no S phase precedes meiosis II.

hot_topics: The five substages of prophase I (leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis) with the one event that defines each
Interphase: G<sub>1</sub>, S, G<sub>2</sub> and the G<sub>0</sub> quiescent stage, with what doubles and what does not
The four stages of mitosis with labelled diagrams and the key features NCERT lists for each
Differences: mitosis versus meiosis, anaphase versus anaphase I, karyokinesis versus cytokinesis, plant versus animal cytokinesis
Chromosome number (N) and DNA content (C) at every stage of the cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis
Synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalent or tetrad, recombination nodule, crossing over, recombinase and chiasmata
Significance of mitosis (growth, nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, repair, meristems) and of meiosis (chromosome number conservation, variation)
Cell cycle durations: 24 hours for a human cell, about 1 hour of M phase, 90 minutes in yeast, interphase over 95 percent

sections.heading: 10.1 Cell Cycle
sections.body:
Every new cell arises from an existing cell by division, and before a cell divides it must do two things: copy its DNA and grow. NCERT defines the cell cycle as the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises the other constituents of the cell and eventually divides into two daughter cells. The three processes, DNA replication, cell growth and cell division, have to happen in a coordinated way so that each progeny cell receives an intact genome. That coordination is what the word 'cycle' captures: a dividing cell goes round the same sequence again and again.

Two numbers from this section are asked directly. A human cell growing in culture divides about once every 24 hours; this is the average cell cycle span for a mammalian cell. The duration varies from organism to organism and from cell type to cell type. Yeast, a single-celled fungus, can complete its whole cycle in about 90 minutes.

Two more ideas belong here. First, a cell that has just been produced by division is small; it grows through the cycle and reaches division size again. Second, DNA replication happens only once per cycle, at one defined point, and the chromosomes are then shared out so that each daughter gets one full copy. Everything else in the chapter is a description of how a cell achieves that. Keep the definition in NCERT's words; a 2-mark 'define the cell cycle' answer is expected to mention genome duplication, synthesis of other constituents, and division into two daughter cells.

formulas.expr: Human cell (in culture): one cycle ≈ 24 hours
where: average cell cycle span of a mammalian cell; this is the answer to NCERT exercise 1
shows that cycle length varies from organism to organism and cell type to cell type

sections.tip: If asked for the average cell cycle span of a mammalian cell, write '24 hours' and add that a human cell in culture divides about once every 24 hours; do not confuse it with the 90-minute yeast cycle.

sections.heading: 10.1.1 Phases of Cell Cycle: Interphase and M Phase
sections.body:
The cycle has two basic phases. The M phase (mitosis phase) is when the actual division happens; it starts with the division of the nucleus (karyokinesis) and usually ends with the division of the cytoplasm (cytokinesis). The interphase is everything between two M phases. It used to be called the resting phase, but nothing rests: the cell grows and replicates its DNA in an orderly way. In a 24-hour human cell cycle, M phase lasts only about an hour; interphase takes more than 95 percent of the cycle.

Interphase is divided into three sub-phases.

  • G1 phase (Gap 1) is the interval between mitosis and the start of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active and grows continuously but does not replicate its DNA.
  • S phase (Synthesis) is when DNA replication occurs. The amount of DNA per cell doubles: if the cell starts with 2C it becomes 4C. The number of chromosomes does not change: a 2n cell stays 2n, each chromosome now having two sister chromatids. In animal cells the centriole also duplicates in the cytoplasm during S phase while DNA replicates in the nucleus.
  • G2 phase (Gap 2) is when proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.

Not every cell keeps cycling. In adult animals some cells, such as heart cells, do not divide at all; many others divide only occasionally, to replace cells lost by injury or death. Cells that do not divide further exit G1 to enter an inactive stage called the quiescent stage, G0. G0 cells remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so by the needs of the organism.

One more sentence from NCERT is a favourite MCQ. In animals, mitotic division is seen only in diploid somatic cells, with a few exceptions where haploid cells divide by mitosis, for example male honey bees. Plants, by contrast, show mitotic divisions in both haploid and diploid cells.

formulas.expr: Interphase (G<sub>1</sub> → S → G<sub>2</sub>) > 95% of the cycle; M phase ≈ 1 h of 24 h
where: DNA doubles 2C → 4C, chromosome number unchanged (2n stays 2n); centriole duplicates
proteins for mitosis synthesised, growth continues

formulas.expr: G<sub>0</sub> = quiescent stage: exit from G<sub>1</sub>, metabolically active, no proliferation
where: heart cells, which do not divide in adults

sections.tip: The trap in every paper: S phase doubles the DNA content, not the chromosome number. Write '2C to 4C, 2n remains 2n' and you have covered the marking point.

sections.heading: 10.2 M Phase: an Overview of Mitosis
sections.body:
M phase is the most dramatic period of the cycle, involving a major reorganisation of virtually all components of the cell. Because the number of chromosomes in the parent and in the progeny cells is the same, mitosis is called equational division. A diploid parent (2n) gives two diploid daughters (2n); the DNA copied in S phase (4C) is shared so each daughter returns to 2C.

For convenience, mitosis is divided into four stages of nuclear division: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. NCERT stresses that this is only for description; mitosis is a continuous process and one stage flows into the next with no sharp boundary. Nuclear division (karyokinesis) is then followed by cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, which completes cell division.

It helps to know what the cell is trying to do at each stage before you learn the details. Prophase packages the replicated chromatin into visible chromosomes and builds a spindle. Metaphase lines every chromosome up at the equator with its two chromatids facing opposite poles. Anaphase splits the centromeres and drags one chromatid of each chromosome to each pole. Telophase rebuilds a nucleus around each set. Then cytokinesis cuts the cell in two.

Examiners ask for the four stages with a labelled diagram of each (NCERT Figure 10.2), and for the 'key features' NCERT lists under metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Learn those lists word for word; they are the marking points. Also remember that mitosis in animals is usually restricted to diploid cells, while in some lower plants and in some social insects haploid cells divide by mitosis.

formulas.expr: Mitosis: 2n (4C) parent → two 2n (2C) daughters; equational division
where: division of the nucleus: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
division of the cytoplasm, completes cell division

sections.tip: Mitosis is one continuous process; if a question asks why it is described in stages, say the stages are for convenience of description and there is no clear boundary between them.

sections.heading: 10.2.1 Prophase
sections.body:
Prophase is the first stage of karyokinesis and follows the S and G2 phases of interphase. At the start the chromosomal material is a diffuse, untangled mass. Through prophase it condenses to form compact mitotic chromosomes. Each chromosome is now seen to be composed of two chromatids attached together at the centromere, because the DNA was replicated in S phase.

The other job of prophase is to start assembling the mitotic spindle. The centrosome, which had duplicated during S phase, now begins to move to the opposite poles of the cell. Each centrosome radiates out microtubules called asters. The two asters together with the spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.

By the end of prophase, the internal organisation of the cell has changed so much that, when viewed under the microscope, the cell does not show Golgi complexes, endoplasmic reticulum, nucleolus or the nuclear envelope. That sentence is asked as a 1-mark item ('which structures are not seen at the end of prophase?').

For a diagram, draw a cell with condensed thread-like chromosomes, each visibly double, scattered inside a fading nuclear envelope, with two centrosomes at opposite poles and short radiating microtubules (asters). Label the chromosome (two chromatids joined at a centromere), the centrosome, the aster and the forming spindle. The marking scheme rewards showing the two chromatids per chromosome and the centrosomes at opposite poles.

formulas.expr: Prophase events: chromatin condenses → compact chromosomes (two chromatids at a centromere); centrosomes move to opposite poles; asters radiate; spindle assembly begins
where: Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus, nuclear envelope

sections.tip: Do not write that the nuclear envelope has fully disappeared in prophase; NCERT places its complete disintegration at the start of metaphase.

sections.heading: 10.2.2 Metaphase
sections.body:
The complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope marks the start of metaphase. With no envelope in the way, the chromosomes spread through the cytoplasm of the cell. By now chromosome condensation is complete, so the chromosomes can be observed clearly; this is the stage at which chromosome morphology is most easily studied, and it is why karyotypes are prepared from metaphase cells.

Each metaphase chromosome is made of two sister chromatids held together by the centromere. On the surface of the centromere are small disc-shaped structures called kinetochores; they are the sites where the spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes. Metaphase is characterised by all the chromosomes coming to lie at the equator of the cell, with one chromatid of each chromosome connected by its kinetochore to spindle fibres from one pole and its sister chromatid connected by its kinetochore to spindle fibres from the opposite pole. The plane of alignment of the chromosomes at metaphase is called the metaphase plate.

NCERT lists two key features of metaphase, and these are the two marks in any 'describe metaphase' question:

  • Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores of chromosomes.
  • Chromosomes are moved to the spindle equator and get aligned along the metaphase plate through spindle fibres to both the poles.

In the diagram, draw the spindle as a football-shaped set of lines between two poles, with all chromosomes lined up in one plane across the middle. Show each chromosome as an X with its centromere on the plate and a fibre from each pole attached at the centromere. Label the spindle fibre, the kinetochore, the metaphase plate and the poles.

formulas.expr: Metaphase: nuclear envelope fully gone; chromosomes maximally condensed; kinetochores attach to spindle fibres; chromosomes aligned at the metaphase plate
where: disc-shaped structure on the surface of the centromere, site of spindle-fibre attachment
plane of alignment of chromosomes at the equator

sections.tip: A common 1-mark question asks the best stage to study chromosome morphology; the answer is metaphase, because condensation is complete and the chromosomes are spread out in one plane.

sections.heading: 10.2.3 Anaphase
sections.body:
At the onset of anaphase, each chromosome arranged at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously at its centromere. The two daughter chromatids, now referred to as the daughter chromosomes of the future daughter nuclei, begin their migration towards the two opposite poles. As each chromosome moves away from the equatorial plate, the centromere of each chromosome is towards the pole and hence leads, while the arms of the chromosome trail behind. This is why anaphase chromosomes look V-shaped, J-shaped or L-shaped depending on the position of the centromere.

NCERT's key features of anaphase:

  • Centromeres split and chromatids separate.
  • Chromatids move to opposite poles.

Two counting points matter in numerical questions. First, the moment the centromeres split, each former chromatid counts as an independent chromosome, so a 2n cell momentarily contains 4n chromosomes in anaphase, although the DNA content is still 4C and will be halved only by cytokinesis. Second, the number of chromosomes reaching each pole equals the original chromosome number of the cell (2n), which is exactly what makes mitosis equational.

Anaphase of mitosis is contrasted with anaphase I of meiosis in almost every exam (NCERT exercise 10). In mitotic anaphase the centromere divides and sister chromatids go to opposite poles, so each pole receives one chromatid from every chromosome. In anaphase I the centromere does not divide; whole homologous chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids, go to opposite poles, so each pole receives one member of every homologous pair. In the diagram, draw the two groups of V-shaped chromatids being pulled apart with the centromere leading, spindle fibres shortening towards the poles, and label the daughter chromosomes, the centromere and the spindle fibres.

formulas.expr: Anaphase: centromere splits → sister chromatids become daughter chromosomes → move to opposite poles, centromere leading, arms trailing
where: momentarily 4n in the cell (2n at each pole); DNA still 4C until cytokinesis

sections.tip: Write 'centromere splits' for anaphase of mitosis and anaphase II, but never for anaphase I; that single word decides the difference question.

sections.heading: 10.2.4 Telophase
sections.body:
Telophase is the final stage of karyokinesis. The chromosomes that have reached their respective poles decondense and lose their individuality. The chromatin material tends to collect in a mass at each of the two poles. Around each cluster the nuclear envelope reassembles, and the structures that had vanished by the end of prophase, the nucleolus, the Golgi complex and the endoplasmic reticulum, reform.

NCERT's key features of telophase, which are the marking points:

  • Chromosomes cluster at opposite spindle poles and their identity is lost as discrete elements.
  • The nuclear envelope assembles around the chromosome clusters.
  • The nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform.

It is useful to see telophase as prophase run backwards: chromosomes condense in prophase and decondense in telophase; the envelope and nucleolus disappear in prophase and reappear in telophase; the spindle is built in prophase and dismantled in telophase. If a question asks you to compare the two, that mirror-image framing gives you three clean differences.

Telophase completes nuclear division: the cell now has two daughter nuclei, each with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus. But it is still one cell. Division of the cytoplasm, cytokinesis, is a separate process that usually begins during telophase. For the diagram, draw a cell that has begun to elongate, with two clusters of decondensing chromatin at the poles, each surrounded by a new nuclear envelope with a nucleolus inside, and label the daughter nuclei, the reforming nuclear envelope and the nucleolus.

formulas.expr: Telophase: chromosomes cluster at poles and decondense; nuclear envelope reassembles; nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform; two daughter nuclei, each 2n
where: the events are the reverse of one another

sections.tip: List all three reforming structures (nucleolus, Golgi complex, ER) together with the nuclear envelope; students usually mention only the envelope and lose a mark.

sections.heading: 10.2.5 Cytokinesis
sections.body:
Mitosis segregates the duplicated chromosomes into two daughter nuclei; this is karyokinesis. The cell itself is divided into two daughter cells by a separate process, cytokinesis, at the end of which cell division is complete. NCERT exercise 2 asks you to distinguish the two: karyokinesis is division of the nucleus and cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm; karyokinesis has four stages and cytokinesis has none; karyokinesis can occur without cytokinesis but cytokinesis normally follows karyokinesis.

Animal and plant cells divide their cytoplasm differently, and this difference is asked in nearly every paper (NCERT exercise 8).

  • In an animal cell, cytokinesis is achieved by the appearance of a furrow in the plasma membrane. The furrow gradually deepens and ultimately joins in the centre, dividing the cell cytoplasm into two. The furrow works from the outside inward, that is, centripetally.
  • In a plant cell, the rigid cell wall cannot furrow. Wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward to meet the existing lateral walls, that is, centrifugally. The formation of the new cell wall begins with a simple precursor called the cell plate, which represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two adjacent cells. The cell plate is laid down from Golgi-derived vesicles that fuse at the equator.

At the time of cytoplasmic division, organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed between the two daughter cells.

Karyokinesis is not always followed by cytokinesis. In some organisms the nucleus divides repeatedly without the cytoplasm dividing, which leads to a multinucleate condition called a syncytium. NCERT's example is the liquid endosperm of coconut, a free-nuclear tissue with many nuclei in a common cytoplasm. This is also the answer to exercise 15: DNA replication without cell division does occur.

formulas.expr: Animal cell: cleavage furrow, deepens centripetally (outside → in). Plant cell: cell plate, grows centrifugally (centre → out), becomes the middle lamella
where: precursor of the new wall, from Golgi vesicles
karyokinesis without cytokinesis; liquid endosperm of coconut

sections.tip: For the 2-mark plant-versus-animal difference, give the two directions (centripetal furrow versus centrifugal cell plate) and the two structures (furrow versus cell plate); that is two full marking points.

sections.heading: 10.3 Significance of Mitosis
sections.body:
Mitosis is usually an equational division restricted to diploid cells, but NCERT reminds you again that in some lower plants and in some social insects haploid cells also divide by mitosis. Its significance is asked as a 3-mark question, and the examiner wants four clear points, ideally with NCERT's examples.

  • Genetic constancy. The two daughter cells produced have the same chromosome number and the same genetic complement as the parent, so all somatic cells of an organism carry identical genetic information.
  • Growth. Mitosis is the basis of the growth of multicellular organisms. A single-celled zygote becomes a body of trillions of cells purely by repeated mitotic divisions.
  • Restoring the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio. As a cell grows, the cytoplasm enlarges but the nucleus does not, which disturbs the ratio between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. Division restores the ratio, so mitosis is a corrective as much as a multiplying process. This point is the one most students miss.
  • Cell repair and replacement. Cells of the upper layer of the epidermis, cells of the lining of the gut, and blood cells are being constantly replaced by mitosis.
  • Continuous growth of plants. Mitotic divisions in the meristematic tissues, the apical meristems and the lateral cambium, result in the continuous growth of plants throughout their life.

Add, if asked for more, that mitosis is the mode of asexual reproduction in many organisms and the means of regeneration, but keep NCERT's points first because the marking scheme is drawn from them.

NCERT exercise 5 asks why mitosis is called equational division. The answer: because the number of chromosomes in the parent and progeny cells is the same, a diploid cell giving two diploid cells, since sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and one goes to each daughter.

formulas.expr: Significance of mitosis: growth; restores nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; repair and replacement (epidermis, gut lining, blood cells); continuous plant growth from apical meristem and lateral cambium; genetic constancy
where: some lower plants, some social insects (male honey bee)

sections.tip: The nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio point is the one that separates a 2/3 from a 3/3 answer; write it explicitly.

sections.heading: 10.4 Meiosis: Overview and Key Features
sections.body:
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of two gametes, each carrying a complete haploid set of chromosomes. Gametes are formed from specialised diploid cells, so there must be a kind of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half. That division is meiosis. Meiosis ensures the production of the haploid phase in the life cycle of sexually reproducing organisms, and fertilisation restores the diploid phase. Meiosis takes place in diploid cells only.

NCERT lists four key features of meiosis; reproduce them in a 'what is meiosis' answer:

  • Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division, called meiosis I and meiosis II, but only a single cycle of DNA replication.
  • Meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase.
  • Meiosis involves the pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between the non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
  • Four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II.

The two divisions each have the four familiar stages. Meiosis I: prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I. Meiosis II: prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, telophase II. Meiosis I is the reductional division, because homologous chromosomes separate and the chromosome number falls from 2n to n. Meiosis II is equational, like mitosis, because sister chromatids separate and the number stays n. In terms of DNA, a 4C cell becomes two 2C cells after meiosis I and then four 1C cells after meiosis II.

Why does the cell need two divisions? Because the one round of replication in S phase leaves each chromosome as two chromatids. Meiosis I halves the number of chromosomes by separating homologues; meiosis II is then needed to separate the chromatids so that each gamete carries single-chromatid chromosomes with 1C DNA.

formulas.expr: Meiosis: one S phase, two divisions; 2n (4C) → meiosis I → two n (2C) cells → meiosis II → four n (1C) cells
where: equational: sister chromatids separate, resembles mitosis

sections.tip: Always say 'reduces the chromosome number to half' and 'four haploid cells'; a definition that says 'produces gametes' without these two phrases does not score full marks.

sections.heading: 10.4.1 Meiosis I: Prophase I and its Five Substages
sections.body:
Prophase I is typically longer and more complex than the prophase of mitosis. It is subdivided into five phases based on the behaviour of the chromosomes: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis. Learn one defining event for each; this list is the single most examined item in the chapter.

  • Leptotene. The chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope as long thin threads. Compaction of chromosomes continues throughout leptotene.
  • Zygotene. Chromosomes start pairing together, a process called synapsis. The paired chromosomes are the homologous chromosomes. Electron micrographs show that synapsis is accompanied by the formation of a complex structure called the synaptonemal complex. The structure formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad (four chromatids). Bivalents are more clearly seen in the next stage.
  • Pachytene. The four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct and clearly appear as tetrads. This stage is characterised by the appearance of recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes. Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between two homologous chromosomes. It is an enzyme-mediated process; the enzyme involved is called recombinase. Crossing over leads to recombination of genetic material on the two chromosomes. Recombination between homologous chromosomes is completed by the end of pachytene, leaving the chromosomes linked at the sites of crossing over.
  • Diplotene. The beginning of diplotene is recognised by the dissolution of the synaptonemal complex. The recombined homologous chromosomes of the bivalents tend to separate from each other except at the sites of crossovers. These X-shaped structures are called chiasmata. In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years.
  • Diakinesis. The final stage of prophase I, marked by terminalisation of chiasmata, the movement of chiasmata towards the ends of the chromosomes. The chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle is assembled to prepare the homologous chromosomes for separation. By the end of diakinesis the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope also breaks down. Diakinesis represents the transition to metaphase I.

A common mnemonic is 'Little Zebras Pace Down Dales' for the order. When you write the 5-mark answer, give each substage its own line with the defining term in bold or underlined: visible threads, synapsis and synaptonemal complex, recombination nodules and crossing over with recombinase, chiasmata and dissolution of the complex, terminalisation and spindle assembly.

formulas.expr: Leptotene: chromosomes visible. Zygotene: synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalent/tetrad. Pachytene: recombination nodules, crossing over (recombinase). Diplotene: synaptonemal complex dissolves, chiasmata. Diakinesis: terminalisation, spindle, nucleolus and envelope gone
where: exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
X-shaped point where homologues stay attached after crossing over
months or years in oocytes of some vertebrates

sections.tip: Zygotene is when the synaptonemal complex forms; pachytene is when crossing over happens; diplotene is when the complex dissolves and chiasmata become visible. Mixing up these three costs marks every year.

sections.heading: 10.4.1 Meiosis I: Metaphase I, Anaphase I, Telophase I and Interkinesis
sections.body:
After diakinesis the nuclear envelope is gone and the spindle is ready. The rest of meiosis I looks like mitosis at a glance, but the unit that moves is the bivalent, not the single chromosome, and that changes everything.

Metaphase I. The bivalent chromosomes align on the equatorial plate. The microtubules from the opposite poles of the spindle attach to the pair of homologous chromosomes; that is, each homologue of a bivalent is attached to fibres from one pole only, so its two sister chromatids face the same pole. Compare mitotic metaphase, where the two chromatids of one chromosome face opposite poles.

Anaphase I. The homologous chromosomes separate, while the sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres. The centromere does not divide. Each pole receives one member of every homologous pair, still double-stranded. The chromosome number is halved here, which is why meiosis I is the reductional division, and which member of each pair goes to which pole is random, which is the independent assortment you will meet in Class 12 genetics.

Telophase I. The nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear, and cytokinesis follows. The result is called a dyad of cells: two haploid cells, each chromosome with two chromatids, each cell with 2C DNA. Although in many cases the chromosomes do undergo some dispersion, they do not reach the extremely extended state of the interphase nucleus.

Interkinesis. The stage between the two meiotic divisions is called interkinesis and is generally short-lived. There is no DNA replication during interkinesis; the chromosomes already have two chromatids from the S phase before meiosis I. Interkinesis is followed by prophase II, a much simpler prophase than prophase I.

The anaphase I versus mitotic anaphase comparison (NCERT exercise 10) is the classic 2 or 3-mark question: in anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate, centromeres do not split, chromatids stay together, and each pole gets n chromosomes; in mitotic anaphase sister chromatids separate, centromeres split, and each pole gets 2n chromosomes.

formulas.expr: Metaphase I: bivalents at the equator, each homologue attached to one pole. Anaphase I: homologues separate, centromeres intact. Telophase I: dyad of two n (2C) cells. Interkinesis: short, no S phase
where: the two cells formed after meiosis I
gap between meiosis I and II; no DNA replication

sections.tip: If a question shows a spindle with paired chromosomes at the equator and asks the stage, answer metaphase I; single chromosomes in a line is metaphase (mitosis) or metaphase II, and the chromosome number in the figure tells you which.

sections.heading: 10.4.2 Meiosis II
sections.body:
Meiosis II is the equational half of meiosis. NCERT says it resembles a normal mitosis, and the stage-by-stage description makes that plain; the one thing to remember is that the cells entering it are already haploid, and no S phase precedes it.

  • Prophase II. Meiosis II is initiated immediately after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before the chromosomes have fully elongated. The nuclear membrane disappears by the end of prophase II, and the chromosomes again become compact.
  • Metaphase II. The chromosomes align at the equator, and the microtubules from opposite poles of the spindle get attached to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. This is the mitotic pattern: the two chromatids of each chromosome face opposite poles.
  • Anaphase II. Begins with the simultaneous splitting of the centromere of each chromosome, which was holding the sister chromatids together, allowing them to move towards opposite poles of the cell by the shortening of the microtubules attached to the kinetochores.
  • Telophase II. Meiosis ends with telophase II, in which the two groups of chromosomes once again get enclosed by a nuclear envelope. Cytokinesis follows, resulting in the formation of a tetrad of cells, that is, four haploid daughter cells, each with n chromosomes and 1C DNA.

Two exercise questions hinge on meiosis II. Exercise 14 asks whether there can be mitosis without DNA replication in S phase. In the normal cycle, no: S-phase replication is what provides the two chromatids that mitosis separates, and without it daughter cells would receive half the genome. But meiosis II is exactly a mitosis-like division not preceded by replication, and that is the best example to give. Exercise 9 asks where the four meiotic products are equal in size and where they are unequal: they are equal in spermatogenesis (four spermatids) and in microsporogenesis (four microspores in a pollen tetrad); they are unequal in oogenesis, where one large ovum and small polar bodies form, and in megasporogenesis, where one of the four megaspores is functional and the other three degenerate.

Note the two uses of the word tetrad in this chapter: a tetrad of four chromatids is the bivalent of prophase I, and a tetrad of cells is the four haploid cells at the end of telophase II. State which one you mean.

formulas.expr: Meiosis II ≈ mitosis on haploid cells: prophase II (envelope gone) → metaphase II (chromatids face opposite poles) → anaphase II (centromere splits) → telophase II (tetrad of four n, 1C cells)
where: oogenesis (ovum + polar bodies), megasporogenesis (one functional megaspore)

sections.tip: In meiosis II the centromere splits (anaphase II); in meiosis I it does not (anaphase I). Any answer that says 'centromere splits' in anaphase I is marked wrong.

sections.heading: 10.5 Significance of Meiosis
sections.body:
NCERT gives two reasons why meiosis matters, and a 2-mark question expects both; a 3-mark question expects both with explanation.

  • Conservation of chromosome number across generations. Meiosis is the mechanism by which the specific chromosome number of each species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms. This sounds paradoxical because meiosis itself reduces the chromosome number by half. The logic: gametes are haploid (n) only because of meiosis; when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote is diploid (2n) again. Without meiosis, the chromosome number would double in every generation, 46 to 92 to 184 in humans.
  • Genetic variability. Meiosis increases genetic variability in the population of organisms from one generation to the next. Two events produce it: crossing over in pachytene, which recombines alleles on homologous chromosomes so that no chromatid is exactly like a parental one, and the random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I, which makes the assortment of maternal and paternal chromosomes into gametes random. These variations are important for the process of evolution, because natural selection acts on variation.

You can add a third point drawn from the start of section 10.4: meiosis produces the haploid phase of the life cycle, that is, the gametes in animals and the spores in plants, while fertilisation restores the diploid phase. Together meiosis and fertilisation make alternation of the two phases possible.

For revision, hold the two divisions side by side. Mitosis keeps things the same: same number, same genes, for growth and repair. Meiosis changes things: half the number, new combinations, for sexual reproduction. Both start from one S phase; mitosis needs one division to share replicated chromosomes, meiosis needs two to first halve the number and then share the chromatids. Every difference in the mitosis-versus-meiosis table comes back to that.

formulas.expr: Significance of meiosis: conserves species chromosome number (n + n → 2n at fertilisation); creates variation by crossing over and random assortment; produces the haploid phase; variation drives evolution
where: reduces the number by half yet conserves it across generations

sections.tip: Write 'conserves the chromosome number across generations' as NCERT phrases it, not 'reduces the chromosome number'; the reduction is the means, the conservation is the significance.

sections.heading: Tracking Chromosome Number (N) and DNA Content (C) through the Cycle (NCERT Exercise 16)
sections.body:
NCERT exercise 16 asks you to analyse every stage of the cell cycle and note how two parameters change: the number of chromosomes per cell (N) and the amount of DNA per cell (C). Case-based questions are built on this, so learn the table rather than working it out under pressure. Use a human cell, 2n = 46, as the running example.

  • G1: 2n = 46 chromosomes, each with one chromatid; 2C DNA.
  • S: DNA replicates; 2C rises to 4C; still 46 chromosomes, now each with two chromatids.
  • G2: 2n = 46, 4C.
  • Mitosis, prophase and metaphase: 46 chromosomes, 4C, 92 chromatids.
  • Mitotic anaphase: centromeres split; 92 chromosomes in the cell, 46 moving to each pole; 4C in the cell, 2C per pole.
  • After telophase and cytokinesis: each daughter has 2n = 46 and 2C. The cycle is back where it started.
  • Meiosis, prophase I and metaphase I: 2n = 46, 4C, 23 bivalents.
  • After meiosis I (dyad): each cell n = 23 chromosomes, each two chromatids; 2C.
  • Metaphase II: n = 23, 2C.
  • After meiosis II (tetrad): each cell n = 23, single chromatids; 1C.

Two rules make any variant easy. First, chromosome number changes only when centromeres split (mitotic anaphase, anaphase II, doubling the count momentarily) or when homologues separate (anaphase I, halving it). Second, DNA content changes only in S phase (doubles) and at each cytokinesis (halves per cell). So if a question says a cell has 8 pg of DNA in G1, it has 16 pg in G2 and metaphase, 8 pg per daughter after mitosis, 8 pg per cell after meiosis I and 4 pg per gamete. If an onion cell has 2n = 16, its metaphase shows 16 chromosomes and 32 chromatids; its gametes carry 8 chromosomes.

Also note the general case of DNA replication without division: polytene chromosomes in Drosophila salivary glands and the multinucleate coconut endosperm both replicate DNA without completing cell division, and the DNA content per nucleus or per cell rises above 4C.

formulas.expr: Mitosis: G<sub>1</sub> 2n 2C → S → G<sub>2</sub> 2n 4C → daughters 2n 2C. Meiosis: 2n 4C → after I: n 2C → after II: n 1C
where: = 2 × chromosome number after S phase, until centromeres split

sections.tip: Count chromosomes by centromeres, never by chromatids. A metaphase cell of a 2n = 16 organism has 16 chromosomes and 32 chromatids, not 32 chromosomes.

key_terms.definition: The sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises the other constituents of the cell and eventually divides into two daughter cells.

The phase between two successive M phases, once called the resting phase, in which the cell grows and replicates its DNA; it occupies more than 95 percent of the cycle and has G<sub>1</sub>, S and G<sub>2</sub> sub-phases.
The interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication; the cell is metabolically active and grows continuously but does not replicate its DNA.
The synthesis phase of interphase in which DNA replicates, doubling the DNA content from 2C to 4C while the chromosome number stays the same; the centriole also duplicates in animal cells.
The second gap of interphase, in which proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.
An inactive stage entered by cells that exit G<sub>1</sub> and do not divide further; such cells remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so by the organism.
The phase of the cycle in which division occurs; it starts with karyokinesis (nuclear division) and usually ends with cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).
Division of the nucleus, achieved in mitosis through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Division of the cytoplasm that follows karyokinesis and completes cell division; by a cleavage furrow in animal cells and by a cell plate in plant cells.
Nuclear division in which the number of chromosomes in the parent and progeny cells is the same, so a diploid cell gives two diploid daughters.
The centrosome, duplicated in S phase, moves to opposite poles during prophase; each centrosome radiates out microtubules called asters, which with the spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.
A small disc-shaped structure on the surface of the centromere that serves as the site of attachment of spindle fibres to the chromosome.
The plane of alignment of the chromosomes at the equator of the spindle during metaphase.
The simple precursor of the new cell wall in a dividing plant cell, formed in the centre and growing outward, which represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two adjacent cells.
A multinucleate condition produced when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, for example the liquid endosperm of coconut.
A specialised division of diploid cells with one round of DNA replication and two sequential divisions, which reduces the chromosome number by half and produces four haploid cells.
The two chromosomes of a pair, one maternal and one paternal, that carry the same genes at the same loci and pair with each other during zygotene.
The pairing of homologous chromosomes that begins in zygotene of prophase I and is accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex.
The complex protein structure seen in electron micrographs that forms between synapsed homologous chromosomes in zygotene and dissolves at the start of diplotene.
The structure formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes; it contains four chromatids, so it is also called a tetrad, and is clearest in pachytene.
A structure that appears in pachytene at the sites where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
The exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of two homologous chromosomes during pachytene, mediated by the enzyme recombinase, which leads to recombination.
The X-shaped structures seen in diplotene at the sites of crossing over, where the recombined homologous chromosomes remain attached after the synaptonemal complex dissolves.
The movement of chiasmata towards the ends of the chromosomes during diakinesis, the last substage of prophase I.
The generally short-lived stage between meiosis I and meiosis II in which no DNA replication takes place.
The two haploid cells formed after meiosis I (dyad) and the four haploid cells formed after meiosis II (tetrad of cells).

formula_sheet.name: Cell cycle durations
formula_sheet.expr: Human cell in culture: about 24 h per cycle, M phase about 1 h; yeast: about 90 min; interphase more than 95 percent of the cycle

formula_sheet.name: Phases in order
formula_sheet.expr: G<sub>1</sub> → S → G<sub>2</sub> → M (prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase → cytokinesis); G<sub>0</sub> branches off G<sub>1</sub>
formula_sheet.note: M phase begins with karyokinesis and usually ends with cytokinesis.

formula_sheet.name: What changes in S phase
formula_sheet.expr: DNA: 2C → 4C; chromosome number: 2n stays 2n; centriole duplicates (animal cells)
formula_sheet.note: Most common trap in the chapter.

formula_sheet.name: N and C through mitosis and meiosis
formula_sheet.expr: G<sub>1</sub>: 2n, 2C; G<sub>2</sub>: 2n, 4C; after mitosis: 2n, 2C each; after meiosis I: n, 2C each; after meiosis II: n, 1C each

formula_sheet.name: Key features of mitotic stages (NCERT lists)
formula_sheet.expr: Metaphase: spindle fibres attach to kinetochores; chromosomes aligned at the metaphase plate. Anaphase: centromeres split, chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. Telophase: chromosomes cluster at poles and lose identity; nuclear envelope assembles; nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform
formula_sheet.note: Write these lists verbatim in describe-the-stage answers.

formula_sheet.name: Prophase I substages
formula_sheet.expr: Leptotene (threads visible) → Zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalent) → Pachytene (recombination nodules, crossing over, recombinase) → Diplotene (complex dissolves, chiasmata; can last months or years in vertebrate oocytes) → Diakinesis (terminalisation, spindle assembled, nucleolus and envelope gone)
formula_sheet.note: Mnemonic: Little Zebras Pace Down Dales.

formula_sheet.name: Anaphase versus anaphase I
formula_sheet.expr: Mitotic anaphase: centromere splits, sister chromatids separate, 2n to each pole. Anaphase I: centromere intact, homologous chromosomes separate, n to each pole (each chromosome still two chromatids)
formula_sheet.note: Anaphase II behaves like mitotic anaphase.

formula_sheet.name: Cytokinesis in animal versus plant cells
formula_sheet.expr: Animal: cleavage furrow in plasma membrane, deepens centripetally. Plant: cell plate from Golgi vesicles at the centre, grows centrifugally, becomes the middle lamella
formula_sheet.note: Organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed between the daughters.

formula_sheet.name: Exceptions to remember
formula_sheet.expr: Haploid mitosis: male honey bee, some lower plants and social insects; plants divide mitotically in haploid and diploid cells. Karyokinesis without cytokinesis: syncytium, liquid endosperm of coconut. Non-dividing cells: heart cells (G<sub>0</sub>)

formula_sheet.name: Equal and unequal meiotic products
formula_sheet.expr: Equal: spermatogenesis (four spermatids), microsporogenesis (four microspores). Unequal: oogenesis (one ovum, polar bodies), megasporogenesis (one functional megaspore, three degenerate)

formula_sheet.name: Significance of mitosis
formula_sheet.expr: Growth; restores nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; repair and replacement of epidermis, gut lining and blood cells; continuous plant growth from apical meristem and lateral cambium; genetic constancy

formula_sheet.name: Significance of meiosis
formula_sheet.expr: Conserves the species chromosome number across generations (gametes n, zygote 2n); increases genetic variability by crossing over and random assortment; variation matters for evolution

formula_sheet.name: Tetrad, two meanings
formula_sheet.expr: Tetrad of chromatids = bivalent in prophase I (four chromatids). Tetrad of cells = four haploid cells after telophase II
formula_sheet.note: State which one you mean in an answer.

diagrams.title: The cell cycle (NCERT Figure 10.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw one large circle and divide it into unequal arcs: a large G<sub>1</sub> arc, then S, then G<sub>2</sub> together making about 23 hours, and a thin M arc of about 1 hour. Inside the M arc write the four stages in order (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) and mark cytokinesis at its end. Draw a short side branch off the G<sub>1</sub> arc leading to a small circle labelled G<sub>0</sub> (quiescent stage). Label interphase as the bracket over G<sub>1</sub> + S + G<sub>2</sub>, and note beside S phase 'DNA replication, 2C → 4C' and beside M phase 'karyokinesis + cytokinesis'. Add 'total about 24 h in a human cell' as a caption.

diagrams.title: Stages of mitosis (NCERT Figure 10.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four cells in a row for one chromosome pair (2n = 4 keeps it readable). Prophase: condensed X-shaped chromosomes inside a fading nuclear envelope, two centrosomes moving to opposite poles with radiating asters. Metaphase: no envelope, spindle fibres from pole to pole, all chromosomes lined up at the metaphase plate with fibres from opposite poles attached to the kinetochores of the two chromatids. Anaphase: centromeres split, V-shaped chromatids pulled to opposite poles with the centromere leading and the arms trailing. Telophase: cell elongated, two chromatin clusters at the poles, nuclear envelope and nucleolus reforming, a cleavage furrow beginning. Label chromosome, chromatid, centromere, kinetochore, spindle fibre, aster, centrosome, metaphase plate, daughter chromosomes, nuclear envelope, nucleolus and furrow.

diagrams.title: Cytokinesis in an animal cell and a plant cell
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two telophase cells side by side. Animal cell: a rounded cell with two daughter nuclei and a cleavage furrow pinching inward from both sides of the plasma membrane; add arrows pointing inward and label 'furrow deepens centripetally'. Plant cell: a rectangular cell with a wall, two daughter nuclei and a line of small vesicles fusing at the centre into a cell plate; add arrows pointing outward from the centre to the lateral walls and label 'cell plate grows centrifugally, becomes middle lamella', with 'Golgi-derived vesicles' at the ends of the plate. Label plasma membrane, cell wall, daughter nuclei, furrow, vesicles and cell plate.

diagrams.title: Substages of prophase I (NCERT Figure 10.3, first row)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw five nuclei in a row for one homologous pair. Leptotene: two long thin separate threads becoming visible. Zygotene: the two homologues lying side by side with a ladder-like synaptonemal complex drawn between them; label the pair as a bivalent. Pachytene: the bivalent as four distinct chromatids (tetrad) with one or two small dark dots on it labelled recombination nodules, and an arrow marking crossing over between non-sister chromatids. Diplotene: the homologues pulling apart but still joined at X-shaped points labelled chiasmata; note 'synaptonemal complex dissolved'. Diakinesis: the chiasmata slid to the ends (terminalisation), chromosomes fully condensed, nuclear envelope broken and spindle fibres appearing. Write the defining event under each panel.

diagrams.title: Synapsis, bivalent and chiasmata (NCERT exercise 7)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw one pair of homologous chromosomes, each as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; shade one homologue and leave the other white so maternal and paternal are distinct. Stage 1: the two homologues side by side with a zip-like synaptonemal complex between them; label synapsis and bivalent (four chromatids). Stage 2: the two inner non-sister chromatids crossing each other at one point; label the crossing point as a chiasma and mark the exchanged segments with the swapped shading to show recombination. Label homologous chromosomes, sister chromatids, non-sister chromatids, centromere, synaptonemal complex and chiasma.

diagrams.title: Metaphase I to telophase I (NCERT Figure 10.3, second row)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three cells with two bivalents (2n = 4). Metaphase I: bivalents lined up at the equator with each homologue attached to spindle fibres from one pole only, so both chromatids of a homologue face the same pole. Anaphase I: the homologues of each pair moving to opposite poles as whole double-stranded chromosomes, centromeres intact; label 'homologous chromosomes separate, sister chromatids stay together'. Telophase I: two nuclei reforming with n = 2 double-stranded chromosomes each and cytokinesis beginning; label the dyad. Label bivalent, homologous chromosomes, spindle fibres, kinetochore, poles and the note 'no S phase in interkinesis'.

diagrams.title: Stages of meiosis II (NCERT Figure 10.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four cells for one of the dyad cells (n = 2, each chromosome two chromatids). Prophase II: chromosomes compact again, nuclear envelope disappearing. Metaphase II: chromosomes in a single line at the equator, fibres from opposite poles attached to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. Anaphase II: centromeres split, chromatids moving to opposite poles. Telophase II: two nuclei each with n single-chromatid chromosomes and cytokinesis; add a bracket to show that both dyad cells do this, giving the tetrad of four haploid cells. Label chromatids, centromere, kinetochore, spindle, nuclear envelope and the four haploid daughter cells.

diagrams.title: Anaphase of mitosis versus anaphase I of meiosis
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two cells side by side, both starting from 2n = 4. Left, mitotic anaphase: four chromosomes had lined up singly; now each centromere has split and eight single chromatids are moving, four to each pole; label 'centromere divides, sister chromatids separate, 2n to each pole'. Right, anaphase I: the two bivalents had lined up as pairs; now four whole chromosomes, each still X-shaped with two chromatids, are moving, two to each pole; label 'centromere intact, homologous chromosomes separate, n to each pole'. Shade maternal and paternal homologues differently so the segregation of pairs is visible.

diagrams.title: Chromosome number and DNA content across the cycle
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal axis with G<sub>1</sub>, S, G<sub>2</sub>, M and then meiosis I and meiosis II marked in order, and a vertical axis for DNA content per cell. Draw a line at 2C through G<sub>1</sub>, rising steadily through S to 4C, flat through G<sub>2</sub> and M, then dropping to 2C at cytokinesis. For meiosis, continue at 4C through prophase I, drop to 2C at the end of meiosis I and to 1C at the end of meiosis II. Above the graph write the chromosome number per cell: 2n through interphase and mitosis, n after meiosis I, n after meiosis II. Label the axes, 1C, 2C, 4C and the two drops.

ncert_questions.q: What is the average cell cycle span for a mammalian cell?
ncert_questions.a: About 24 hours. A human cell growing in culture divides about once every 24 hours. Of this, M phase takes only about an hour and interphase more than 95 percent of the cycle. The span varies between organisms and cell types; yeast completes its cycle in about 90 minutes.

Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus. It is achieved through the four stages prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and results in two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent (in mitosis). Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows karyokinesis and completes cell division; it has no stages, and occurs by a cleavage furrow in animal cells and by a cell plate in plant cells. Karyokinesis can occur without cytokinesis, giving a multinucleate syncytium such as the liquid endosperm of coconut, but cytokinesis normally follows karyokinesis. Together they make up the M phase.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the events taking place during interphase.
ncert_questions.a:
Interphase is the period between two successive M phases in which the cell prepares for division by cell growth and DNA replication in an orderly manner. It occupies more than 95 percent of the cell cycle and has three sub-phases.

  • G1 phase: the interval between mitosis and the start of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active, grows continuously and synthesises RNA and proteins, but does not replicate DNA.
  • S phase: DNA replication takes place. The amount of DNA per cell doubles from 2C to 4C, but the chromosome number does not change (2n remains 2n); each chromosome now has two sister chromatids. In animal cells the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm during this phase.
  • G2 phase: proteins required for mitosis are synthesised and cell growth continues.

Cells that will not divide further exit G1 into the quiescent G0 stage, where they stay metabolically active without proliferating.

ncert_questions.q: What is G<sub>0</sub> (quiescent phase) of cell cycle?
ncert_questions.a: G0 is the inactive stage of the cell cycle entered by cells that do not divide further. Such cells exit the G1 phase and enter G0, where they remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so depending on the requirement of the organism. Heart cells of adult animals are an example of cells that do not divide; many other adult cells divide only occasionally, to replace cells lost by injury or death.

ncert_questions.q: Why is mitosis called equational division?
ncert_questions.a: Mitosis is called equational division because the number of chromosomes in the parent cell and in the two progeny cells is the same. The DNA is replicated in S phase so that each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids; in anaphase the centromeres split and one chromatid of every chromosome goes to each pole. Each daughter nucleus therefore receives exactly the parental chromosome number (2n gives 2n and 2n) and an identical genetic complement.

ncert_questions.q: Name the stage of cell cycle at which one of the following events occur: (i) Chromosomes are moved to spindle equator. (ii) Centromere splits and chromatids separate. (iii) Pairing between homologous chromosomes takes place. (iv) Crossing over between homologous chromosomes takes place.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Metaphase (of mitosis; also metaphase I and II of meiosis).
(ii) Anaphase of mitosis (also anaphase II of meiosis; not anaphase I).
(iii) Zygotene of prophase I of meiosis (synapsis).
(iv) Pachytene of prophase I of meiosis.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the following: (a) synapsis (b) bivalent (c) chiasmata. Draw a diagram to illustrate your answer.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes that occurs during zygotene of prophase I. Electron micrographs show that it is accompanied by the formation of a complex structure between the paired chromosomes called the synaptonemal complex.

(b) Bivalent is the structure formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes. As each chromosome has two chromatids, the bivalent contains four chromatids and is also called a tetrad. Bivalents become clearly visible in pachytene.

(c) Chiasmata are the X-shaped structures seen in diplotene at the sites of crossing over. After the synaptonemal complex dissolves, the recombined homologous chromosomes tend to separate but remain attached at these points. During diakinesis the chiasmata move to the ends of the chromosomes (terminalisation).

Diagram: draw two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, lying side by side with a ladder-like synaptonemal complex between them (synapsis, bivalent); then draw the same pair with two non-sister chromatids crossing at one point labelled chiasma, with the exchanged segments shaded to show crossing over.

ncert_questions.q: How does cytokinesis in plant cells differ from that in animal cells?
ncert_questions.a: In an animal cell cytokinesis occurs by a cleavage furrow: a furrow appears in the plasma membrane, gradually deepens from the periphery towards the centre (centripetally) and finally joins in the middle to divide the cytoplasm into two. In a plant cell the rigid wall prevents furrowing. Instead, wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward (centrifugally) to meet the existing lateral walls. It begins with a simple precursor, the cell plate, formed from Golgi-derived vesicles, which represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two daughter cells. In both cases organelles such as mitochondria and plastids get distributed between the two daughters.

ncert_questions.q: Find examples where the four daughter cells from meiosis are equal in size and where they are found unequal in size.
ncert_questions.a:
Equal in size: spermatogenesis in animals, where a primary spermatocyte forms four equal haploid spermatids; and microsporogenesis in plants, where a microspore mother cell forms a tetrad of four equal microspores (pollen grains).

Unequal in size: oogenesis in animals, where a primary oocyte produces one large ovum and small polar bodies because cytokinesis is unequal; and megasporogenesis in plants, where the four megaspores are formed in a linear tetrad but usually only one enlarges to become the functional megaspore while the other three degenerate.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish anaphase of mitosis from anaphase I of meiosis.
ncert_questions.a:
• In anaphase of mitosis the centromere of each chromosome splits; in anaphase I the centromere does not divide.
  • In mitotic anaphase the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles as daughter chromosomes; in anaphase I the homologous chromosomes separate while the sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres.
  • In mitotic anaphase each pole receives the full chromosome number (2n), each chromosome single-stranded; in anaphase I each pole receives half the number (n), each chromosome still two-stranded.
  • Mitotic anaphase is preceded by single chromosomes aligned at the metaphase plate; anaphase I is preceded by bivalents aligned at the equator, and the separating homologues carry recombined segments from crossing over.

ncert_questions.q: List the main differences between mitosis and meiosis.
ncert_questions.a:
• Cells: mitosis occurs in somatic cells (and in haploid cells of some organisms); meiosis occurs only in diploid reproductive (germ) cells.
  • Number of divisions: mitosis has one nuclear and one cell division; meiosis has two sequential divisions (meiosis I and II) after a single S phase.
  • Chromosome number: mitosis is equational, daughters have the parental number (2n to 2n); meiosis is reductional, daughters have half the number (2n to n).
  • Daughter cells: mitosis gives two cells genetically identical to the parent; meiosis gives four cells genetically different from the parent and from each other.
  • Prophase: mitotic prophase is short and simple; prophase I is long and complex with five substages (leptotene to diakinesis).
  • Pairing and crossing over: absent in mitosis; synapsis, bivalent formation, crossing over and chiasmata occur in prophase I of meiosis.
  • Anaphase: in mitosis centromeres split and sister chromatids separate; in anaphase I centromeres stay intact and homologous chromosomes separate (chromatids separate only in anaphase II).
  • Significance: mitosis is for growth, repair and asexual reproduction; meiosis is for gamete or spore formation, conserving the chromosome number across generations and producing variation.

ncert_questions.q: What is the significance of meiosis?
ncert_questions.a:
• Meiosis is the mechanism by which the specific chromosome number of each species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, even though the process itself reduces the number by half: meiosis produces haploid gametes, and fertilisation of two gametes restores the diploid number in the zygote.
  • It increases genetic variability in the population from one generation to the next, through crossing over between homologous chromosomes in pachytene and the random assortment of homologues in anaphase I. These variations are important for the process of evolution.
  • It produces the haploid phase (gametes in animals, spores in plants) of the life cycle of sexually reproducing organisms.

ncert_questions.q: Discuss with your teacher about (i) haploid insects and lower plants where cell division occurs, and (ii) some haploid cells in higher plants where cell division does not occur.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) In some insects and lower plants haploid cells divide by mitosis. The male honey bee (drone) develops from an unfertilised egg by parthenogenesis and is haploid; all its body cells arise by mitosis of haploid cells. In lower plants such as mosses and many algae, the gametophyte is haploid and grows by mitotic divisions of haploid cells; in these organisms the haploid phase is the dominant, long-lived phase.

(ii) In higher plants some haploid cells do not divide further: the male gametes (sperm cells) in the pollen tube, the egg cell and the synergids of the embryo sac, and the vegetative cell of the pollen grain, which only forms the pollen tube. The egg divides only after fertilisation, when it has become the diploid zygote.

ncert_questions.q: Can there be mitosis without DNA replication in 'S' phase?
ncert_questions.a: In the normal cell cycle, no. S phase replication provides each chromosome with two identical sister chromatids, and mitosis works by separating these chromatids so that each daughter gets a complete genome. If the DNA were not replicated the daughter cells would receive half the genetic material and could not survive. However, a mitosis-like division without a preceding S phase does occur in meiosis II: the cells produced by meiosis I enter prophase II after a short interkinesis with no DNA replication, because their chromosomes already have two chromatids from the S phase before meiosis I.

ncert_questions.q: Can there be DNA replication without cell division?
ncert_questions.a: Yes. When karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis the nucleus divides repeatedly, with DNA replicating each time, but the cell does not divide; this produces a multinucleate syncytium such as the liquid endosperm of coconut. DNA can also replicate repeatedly without even nuclear division (endoreduplication), as in the polytene chromosomes of the salivary glands of Drosophila, where many identical chromatids lie side by side in one giant chromosome.

ncert_questions.q: Analyse the events during every stage of cell cycle and notice how the following two parameters change: (i) number of chromosomes (N) per cell, (ii) amount of DNA content (C) per cell.
ncert_questions.a:
Take a diploid cell with 2n chromosomes and 2C DNA in G1.

  • G1: N = 2n, DNA = 2C.
  • S: DNA doubles to 4C; N stays 2n, each chromosome now two chromatids.
  • G2: N = 2n, DNA = 4C.
  • Mitosis, prophase and metaphase: N = 2n, DNA = 4C.
  • Anaphase: centromeres split, so 4n chromatids-now-chromosomes in the cell, 2n heading to each pole; DNA 4C in the cell.
  • After telophase and cytokinesis: each daughter N = 2n, DNA = 2C.
  • Meiosis, prophase I and metaphase I: N = 2n, DNA = 4C.
  • After meiosis I: each cell N = n (two-chromatid chromosomes), DNA = 2C.
  • After meiosis II: each cell N = n (single-chromatid chromosomes), DNA = 1C.

For a human cell: 46 chromosomes and 2C in G1; 46 and 4C in G2; 46 and 2C in each mitotic daughter; 23 and 2C after meiosis I; 23 and 1C in each gamete.

pyq.q: The enzyme recombinase is required at which stage of meiosis?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Crossing over occurs in pachytene at the recombination nodules, and it is an enzyme-mediated process using recombinase.

pyq.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of the S phase?
options: DNA content per cell doubles from 2C to 4C
The number of chromosomes per cell doubles
The centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm of animal cells
DNA replication begins in the nucleus
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: S phase doubles the DNA content but not the chromosome number; a 2n cell remains 2n, each chromosome now having two chromatids.

pyq.q: The stage of prophase I that can last for months or years in the oocytes of some vertebrates is
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT states that in oocytes of some vertebrates diplotene can last for months or years; the oocyte is arrested with visible chiasmata.

pyq.q: Chromosome morphology is best studied at
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In metaphase chromosome condensation is complete and the chromosomes lie spread out in one plane at the metaphase plate, so their morphology is most easily observed.

pyq.q: In a 24-hour cell cycle of a human cell, the approximate duration of M phase is
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The M phase lasts only about an hour; interphase, occupying more than 95 percent of the cycle, takes the remaining 23 hours or so.

pyq.q: During which stage of mitosis are the Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum, nucleolus and nuclear envelope no longer visible under the microscope?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT states that cells at the end of prophase do not show Golgi complexes, ER, nucleolus and the nuclear envelope; these reform in telophase.

pyq.q: In which of the following does the centromere NOT divide?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay joined at the centromere; the centromere splits in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II.

pyq.q: The formation of a cell plate during cytokinesis of a plant cell is characterised by
options: A furrow that deepens from the periphery to the centre
Wall formation starting at the centre and growing outward to the lateral walls
Constriction of the plasma membrane by microfilaments
Formation of the wall before karyokinesis is complete
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In plant cells wall formation starts in the centre as the cell plate, which grows outward (centrifugally) to meet the existing lateral walls and becomes the middle lamella.

pyq.q: A cell has 8 chromosomes in G<sub>1</sub>. The number of chromatids in this cell at metaphase of mitosis and the number of chromosomes in each gamete formed from it by meiosis are, respectively,
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: After S phase each of the 8 chromosomes has two chromatids, giving 16 chromatids at metaphase; meiosis halves the number, so gametes have 4 chromosomes.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Meiosis I is called reductional division. Reason (R): In anaphase I the centromeres split and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Meiosis I is reductional because homologous chromosomes separate and the number falls from 2n to n; the centromeres do not split in anaphase I, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The DNA content of a cell doubles during the S phase but its chromosome number stays the same. Reason (R): After replication each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at a single centromere.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Chromosomes are counted by centromeres; replication produces two chromatids sharing one centromere, so DNA becomes 4C while 2n stays 2n.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Cells in the G<sub>0</sub> stage do not divide. Reason (R): Cells in G<sub>0</sub> are metabolically inactive.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: G<sub>0</sub> cells have exited G<sub>1</sub> and do not proliferate, but NCERT states that they remain metabolically active, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Meiosis II resembles a normal mitosis. Reason (R): In anaphase II the centromere of each chromosome splits and the sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Meiosis II is equational: chromatids face opposite poles in metaphase II and separate in anaphase II when the centromere splits, exactly as in mitosis.

pyq.q: Define interkinesis. Why is it different from interphase?
pyq.answer: Interkinesis is the generally short-lived stage between the two meiotic divisions, that is, between telophase I and prophase II. It differs from interphase because there is no DNA replication (no S phase) during interkinesis; the chromosomes entering meiosis II already have two chromatids from the S phase that preceded meiosis I, and they do not decondense to the fully extended interphase state.

pyq.q: What is a kinetochore? State its role in cell division.
pyq.answer: A kinetochore is a small disc-shaped structure present on the surface of the centromere of a chromosome. It is the site of attachment of the spindle fibres. In metaphase, spindle fibres from one pole attach to the kinetochore of one chromatid and fibres from the opposite pole to the kinetochore of its sister chromatid, so the chromosome is aligned at the metaphase plate and, in anaphase, the chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.

pyq.q: Name the stage of meiosis in which (i) the synaptonemal complex is formed, (ii) the synaptonemal complex dissolves, (iii) recombination nodules appear, (iv) terminalisation of chiasmata occurs.
pyq.answer: (i) Zygotene. (ii) Diplotene. (iii) Pachytene. (iv) Diakinesis.

pyq.q: A diploid organism has 2n = 20. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids are present in one of its cells at metaphase I of meiosis? How many chromosomes will each cell have at the end of meiosis I and at the end of meiosis II?
pyq.answer: At metaphase I the cell has 2n = 20 chromosomes, each with two chromatids, so 40 chromatids arranged as 10 bivalents. At the end of meiosis I each of the two cells has n = 10 chromosomes (each still two chromatids, 20 chromatids). At the end of meiosis II each of the four cells has 10 chromosomes, each a single chromatid.

pyq.q: What is a syncytium? Give one example.
pyq.answer: A syncytium is a multinucleate condition that arises when karyokinesis (nuclear division) is not followed by cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm), so that repeated nuclear divisions leave many nuclei in a common cytoplasm. Example: the liquid endosperm of coconut, a free-nuclear endosperm formed by repeated nuclear divisions without wall formation.

pyq.q: Describe the events of pachytene and diplotene of prophase I.
pyq.answer:
Pachytene: the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct and clearly appear as tetrads. This stage is characterised by the appearance of recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes. Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between two homologous chromosomes; it is enzyme-mediated by recombinase and leads to recombination of genetic material on the two chromosomes. Recombination is completed by the end of pachytene, leaving the chromosomes linked at the sites of crossing over.

Diplotene: its beginning is recognised by the dissolution of the synaptonemal complex. The recombined homologous chromosomes of the bivalents tend to separate from each other except at the sites of crossovers, which appear as X-shaped structures called chiasmata. In oocytes of some vertebrates diplotene can last for months or years.

pyq.q: Describe metaphase of mitosis and state its key features. Why is it the best stage to study chromosomes?
pyq.answer:
Metaphase begins with the complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope, after which the chromosomes spread through the cytoplasm. Condensation is complete, so each chromosome is clearly seen as two sister chromatids held together at the centromere, on whose surface lie small disc-shaped kinetochores. Spindle fibres from one pole attach to the kinetochore of one chromatid and fibres from the opposite pole to the kinetochore of its sister, and all chromosomes come to lie at the equator in a plane called the metaphase plate.

Key features: (i) spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores of the chromosomes; (ii) chromosomes are moved to the spindle equator and aligned along the metaphase plate through spindle fibres to both poles.

It is the best stage to study chromosome morphology because condensation is maximal and the chromosomes are spread out in a single plane, so their number, size and centromere position can be observed and counted; karyotypes are prepared from metaphase cells.

pyq.q: Write three points of significance of mitosis, giving NCERT examples.
pyq.answer:
• Growth: mitosis is the basis of growth of multicellular organisms; a single-celled zygote grows into the adult body by repeated mitotic divisions, and mitotic divisions in the meristematic tissues (apical meristem and lateral cambium) allow continuous growth of plants throughout life.
  • Restoring the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio: as a cell grows the cytoplasm enlarges more than the nucleus, disturbing the ratio between them; division restores it.
  • Repair and replacement: cells of the upper layer of the epidermis, cells of the lining of the gut and blood cells are constantly replaced by mitosis.
  • (Also) genetic constancy: the daughter cells have the same chromosome number and genetic make-up as the parent, so all somatic cells carry identical information; mitosis is also the basis of asexual reproduction and regeneration.

pyq.q: Explain why meiosis is said to conserve the chromosome number of a species even though it reduces the chromosome number by half. How does meiosis contribute to variation?
pyq.answer:
Sexual reproduction involves fusion of two gametes. If gametes carried the full diploid number, the zygote would have double the number and the chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis reduces the number in the gametes to half (n), so that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote regains the diploid number (n + n = 2n). Thus the reduction is the means by which the specific chromosome number of the species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms.

Meiosis increases genetic variability in two ways: crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during pachytene produces chromatids with new combinations of alleles, and the random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I means maternal and paternal chromosomes are assorted randomly into gametes. Every gamete is therefore genetically different, and these variations are important for evolution.

pyq.q: Describe cytokinesis in a plant cell. What happens if karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis?
pyq.answer:
A plant cell has a rigid wall, so it cannot divide by a furrow. Instead, wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward (centrifugally) to meet the existing lateral walls. The new wall begins as a simple precursor called the cell plate, formed by the fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles at the equator of the cell; the cell plate represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two adjacent daughter cells, and the primary walls are then laid down on either side of it. During the division, organelles such as mitochondria and plastids get distributed between the two daughter cells.
