If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, the nucleus divides repeatedly while the cytoplasm does not, giving a multinucleate condition called a syncytium, for example the liquid endosperm of coconut.

pyq.q: Describe the four stages of karyokinesis in mitosis with the help of labelled diagrams.
pyq.answer:
Mitosis is a continuous process but is described in four stages for convenience.

Prophase: follows S and G2. The chromosomal material condenses to form compact mitotic chromosomes, each seen to be composed of two chromatids attached at the centromere. The centrosome, duplicated in S phase, moves to opposite poles and each radiates microtubules called asters; the two asters and the spindle fibres make up the mitotic apparatus. By the end of prophase the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are not seen.

Metaphase: begins with complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope; the chromosomes spread through the cytoplasm and are fully condensed. Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores (disc-shaped structures on the centromeres), one chromatid to fibres from one pole and its sister to fibres from the opposite pole, and all chromosomes are aligned at the equator along the metaphase plate.

Anaphase: each chromosome at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously at the centromere; the two daughter chromatids, now daughter chromosomes, migrate to opposite poles with the centromere leading and the arms trailing.

Telophase: the chromosomes cluster at opposite spindle poles, decondense and lose their identity as discrete elements; the nuclear envelope assembles around each chromosome cluster; the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm.

Diagrams: four cells as in NCERT Figure 10.2: prophase with condensed double chromosomes, centrosomes and asters; metaphase with chromosomes on the metaphase plate and spindle fibres at the kinetochores; anaphase with V-shaped chromatids moving to the poles; telophase with two reforming nuclei and a beginning furrow. Label chromatid, centromere, kinetochore, spindle fibre, aster, metaphase plate, daughter chromosomes, nuclear envelope and nucleolus.

pyq.q: Describe the five substages of prophase I of meiosis. Draw a diagram showing a bivalent with chiasmata.
pyq.answer:
Prophase I is longer and more complex than mitotic prophase and has five substages based on chromosomal behaviour.

  • Leptotene: chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope as thin threads; compaction continues throughout the stage.
  • Zygotene: homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis), accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex between them; the paired structure is a bivalent or tetrad.
  • Pachytene: the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct as tetrads; recombination nodules appear at the sites where crossing over, the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, occurs; the process is mediated by the enzyme recombinase and is completed by the end of pachytene, leaving the chromosomes linked at the crossover sites.
  • Diplotene: begins with dissolution of the synaptonemal complex; the recombined homologues tend to separate except at the crossover sites, which appear as X-shaped chiasmata; in oocytes of some vertebrates this stage can last months or years.
  • Diakinesis: marked by terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes are fully condensed, the meiotic spindle is assembled, and the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; it is the transition to metaphase I.

Diagram: two homologous chromosomes (shade one), each with two sister chromatids, lying side by side; two non-sister chromatids crossing at one or two X-shaped points labelled chiasmata; label homologous chromosomes, sister chromatids, non-sister chromatids, centromere, bivalent and the exchanged (recombined) segments.

pyq.q: Describe the stages of meiosis II. In what ways does meiosis II resemble mitosis, and in what way does it differ?
pyq.answer:
Meiosis II follows a short interkinesis in which there is no DNA replication.

  • Prophase II: initiated immediately after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before the chromosomes have fully elongated; the nuclear membrane disappears by the end of the stage and the chromosomes become compact again.
  • Metaphase II: the chromosomes align at the equator, and microtubules from opposite poles of the spindle attach to the kinetochores of the sister chromatids.
  • Anaphase II: begins with the simultaneous splitting of the centromere of each chromosome, which was holding the sister chromatids together, allowing them to move to opposite poles by shortening of the microtubules attached to the kinetochores.
  • Telophase II: the two groups of chromosomes are again enclosed by a nuclear envelope; cytokinesis follows, forming a tetrad of four haploid daughter cells.

Resemblance to mitosis: it is an equational division; the sister chromatids of each chromosome face opposite poles at metaphase II, the centromere splits at anaphase II and the chromatids separate, so the chromosome number of the cell entering it (n) is retained in the products; there is no pairing of homologues or crossing over.

Difference: the cells entering meiosis II are haploid, no S phase precedes it (the chromatids were formed in the S phase before meiosis I), the chromatids are not identical because of crossing over in pachytene, and the products are four haploid (n, 1C) gametes or spores rather than two diploid cells.

pyq.q:
A student examined dividing cells from an onion root tip (2n = 16) and from an onion flower bud. In one slide she saw a cell with chromosomes lined up singly at the equator, each attached to fibres from both poles. In another she saw 8 paired structures at the equator, each attached to fibres from only one pole. In a third she saw chromosomes moving to the poles with their centromeres intact.
(i) Identify the stage in the first slide and state the number of chromatids in that cell.
(ii) Identify the stage in the second slide and name the paired structures.
(iii) Identify the stage in the third slide and state how many chromosomes reach each pole.
(iv) How much DNA, relative to the G1 content, does each cell of the flower bud have after the second slide's division is complete?
pyq.answer:
(i) Metaphase of mitosis (root tip, somatic tissue). The cell has 16 chromosomes, each with two chromatids, so 32 chromatids.
(ii) Metaphase I of meiosis (flower bud, reproductive tissue). The 8 paired structures are bivalents or tetrads, each formed by two synapsed homologous chromosomes.
(iii) Anaphase I of meiosis: homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay attached at the centromere, so 8 chromosomes (each two-stranded) reach each pole.
(iv) After meiosis I each cell has half the G2 DNA, that is 2C, the same amount as a G1 cell (n = 8 chromosomes, each still two chromatids). Only after meiosis II does it fall to 1C.

pyq.q:
The graph of DNA content per cell against time for a human cell shows 2C during the first 11 hours, a rise to 4C over the next 8 hours, a plateau at 4C for 4 hours, and a sudden fall to 2C in the last hour of a 24-hour cycle.
(i) Name the phases corresponding to the four parts of the graph.
(ii) How many chromosomes and chromatids does the cell have during the plateau?
(iii) Why is there no rise in chromosome number during the rising part of the graph?
(iv) If this cell exited the cycle just before the rising part and stopped dividing, what stage would it be in? State one property of cells in that stage.
pyq.answer:
(i) 2C for 11 h: G1 phase; rise to 4C: S phase (DNA replication); plateau at 4C: G2 phase (and prophase to anaphase of mitosis); fall to 2C in the last hour: M phase, when cytokinesis divides the 4C between two daughter cells.
(ii) 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids (each chromosome has two sister chromatids after S phase).
(iii) In S phase each chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids that remain joined at one centromere; chromosomes are counted by centromeres, so the DNA doubles but the number remains 46.
(iv) G0, the quiescent stage, entered by exiting G1. Cells in G0 remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on to do so by the organism (for example heart cells).

practice_mcq.q: The synaptonemal complex is formed during
practice_mcq.explanation: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes in zygotene is accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex; it dissolves in diplotene.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following occurs in the G<sub>2</sub> phase?
options: Synthesis of proteins needed for mitosis
practice_mcq.explanation: In G<sub>2</sub> proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while growth continues; DNA and centriole duplication belong to S phase.

options: Two asters and the spindle fibres
practice_mcq.explanation: Each centrosome radiates microtubules called asters; the two asters together with the spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.

practice_mcq.q: Terminalisation of chiasmata takes place in
practice_mcq.explanation: Diakinesis, the last substage of prophase I, is marked by terminalisation of chiasmata, full condensation and spindle assembly.

practice_mcq.q: In which of the following do haploid cells divide by mitosis?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives the male honey bee as an exception in animals where haploid cells divide by mitosis; heart cells do not divide.

practice_mcq.q: The 'dyad of cells' is formed at the end of
practice_mcq.explanation: Cytokinesis after telophase I produces two haploid cells, the dyad; meiosis II produces the tetrad of four cells.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about interkinesis is correct?
options: DNA replicates in preparation for meiosis II
It is a long stage equivalent to interphase
It is generally short and has no DNA replication
practice_mcq.explanation: Interkinesis between meiosis I and II is generally short-lived and there is no DNA replication during it.

practice_mcq.q: The cell plate formed during plant cytokinesis represents the
practice_mcq.explanation: The cell plate is the precursor of the new wall and represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two adjacent daughter cells.

practice_mcq.q: A cell with 2n = 12 undergoes mitosis. The number of chromosomes moving towards each pole during anaphase is
practice_mcq.explanation: After the centromeres split, one chromatid of each of the 12 chromosomes moves to each pole, so 12 daughter chromosomes reach each pole.

practice_mcq.q: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between
practice_mcq.explanation: Recombination nodules in pachytene mark the sites of crossing over between non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair.

practice_mcq.q: The percentage of the cell cycle occupied by interphase is
practice_mcq.explanation: Interphase lasts more than 95 percent of the cycle; M phase is only about one hour of a 24-hour human cycle.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
practice_mcq.explanation: Recombination nodules appear in pachytene; chiasmata become visible in diplotene, when the synaptonemal complex that formed in zygotene dissolves.
NCERT states that the centrosome, which had undergone duplication during S phase, begins to move to opposite poles in prophase.

practice_mcq.q: An oocyte arrested for years before ovulation is held in
practice_mcq.explanation: In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a significance of mitosis listed in NCERT?
options: Replacement of gut lining and blood cells
practice_mcq.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells; production of variation is a significance of meiosis, through crossing over and random assortment.

options: Before both meiosis I and meiosis II
practice_mcq.explanation: Meiosis has a single cycle of DNA replication, in the S phase before meiosis I; no replication occurs in interkinesis.

practice_mcq.q: The liquid endosperm of coconut is an example of
practice_mcq.explanation: Repeated nuclear divisions without division of the cytoplasm produce the multinucleate syncytium of the coconut's liquid endosperm.

practice_mcq.q: Which set represents the correct sequence of stages of meiosis I?
options: Prophase I, anaphase I, metaphase I, telophase I
practice_mcq.explanation: The five substages of prophase I in order are leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis; option (b) swaps zygotene and pachytene.

common_mistakes: Writing that the chromosome number doubles in S phase. Only the DNA content doubles (2C to 4C); the chromosome number stays 2n because the two chromatids share one centromere. Examiners deduct the full mark for this.
Saying the centromere splits in anaphase I. It does not; homologous chromosomes separate with sister chromatids still joined. The centromere splits in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II only.

Mixing up the three middle substages of prophase I: the synaptonemal complex forms in zygotene, crossing over and recombination nodules belong to pachytene, and chiasmata become visible in diplotene when the complex dissolves. Terminalisation is diakinesis.
Calling G<sub>0</sub> a dead or inactive stage. NCERT says G<sub>0</sub> cells remain metabolically active; they simply do not proliferate unless called on to do so.

Answering the plant-versus-animal cytokinesis question with only 'cell plate' and 'furrow'. Give the directions too: the cell plate grows from the centre outward (centrifugal), the furrow deepens from the periphery inward (centripetal).

Placing the disappearance of the nuclear envelope in prophase. NCERT marks the complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope as the start of metaphase; at the end of prophase it is simply no longer visible.

Omitting the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio when asked for the significance of mitosis, and omitting 'conservation of chromosome number across generations' when asked for the significance of meiosis; both are the specific NCERT points the marking scheme looks for.
Counting chromatids as chromosomes in numerical questions. Count by centromeres: a 2n = 16 cell at metaphase has 16 chromosomes and 32 chromatids; each gamete gets 8 chromosomes.

Drawing metaphase I with single chromosomes in a line, or drawing mitotic metaphase with paired chromosomes. Metaphase I shows bivalents with each homologue attached to one pole; mitotic metaphase shows single chromosomes with the two chromatids attached to opposite poles.
strategy:
This chapter is learned in layers, and the exam tests each layer separately. Start with the skeleton: the cycle (G1, S, G2, M, G0), the four stages of mitosis plus cytokinesis, then meiosis I with the five substages of prophase I, then meiosis II. Draw the whole thing once from memory as a flowchart with the chromosome number and DNA content written beside every stage. If you can produce that page unaided, the case-based and numerical questions are already answered.

Next, memorise NCERT's exact wording for the 'key features' of metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and the one defining event of each prophase I substage. These are lifted straight into marking schemes, so match the vocabulary: kinetochore, metaphase plate, synaptonemal complex, recombination nodule, recombinase, chiasmata, terminalisation, interkinesis, dyad, tetrad.

Third, practise the four difference tables until you can write each in under three minutes: karyokinesis versus cytokinesis, plant versus animal cytokinesis, anaphase versus anaphase I, and mitosis versus meiosis (at least six points). Each is a near-certain 2 or 3-mark question, and the mitosis-versus-meiosis table is often the 5-mark question.

Fourth, the diagrams. Practise the four mitosis stages and the meiosis I stages as clean line drawings for 2n = 4 with every label from the diagrams section. Shade maternal and paternal homologues differently in meiosis figures so the examiner can see that you know pairs separate in anaphase I. A labelled diagram with correct stage names can carry half the marks of a 5-mark question even if the description is thin.

Finally, solve all 16 NCERT exercise questions in writing; exercises 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 16 appear in school papers almost verbatim. Give this chapter about four hours of first study and one hour of revision with the checklist below the night before the exam.
revision_checklist: I can define the cell cycle in NCERT's words and state 24 h (human), about 1 h M phase, 90 min (yeast), interphase over 95 percent.
I can state what happens in G<sub>1</sub>, S and G<sub>2</sub>, including 2C to 4C with 2n unchanged and centriole duplication in S.
I can define G<sub>0</sub> and say that its cells are metabolically active but do not proliferate; heart cells are the example.
I can distinguish karyokinesis from cytokinesis and give the coconut endosperm syncytium as karyokinesis without cytokinesis.
I can describe prophase of mitosis, including centrosome movement, asters, the mitotic apparatus, and the four structures not seen at its end.

I can write the key features of metaphase (kinetochore attachment, metaphase plate), anaphase (centromere splits, chromatids to poles) and telophase (clusters, envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform).
I can draw the four stages of mitosis for 2n = 4 with all labels.
I can compare cytokinesis in animal (centripetal furrow) and plant (centrifugal cell plate, middle lamella, Golgi vesicles) cells.
